title: The Efficiency Correlation

scenario.situation: A cross-plant analysis shows that cost-per-unit and defects-per-unit correlate strongly (r = 0.81) across the company's 14 manufacturing plants.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The operations team concludes that cost-cutting initiatives will also reduce defects — two birds, one stone.
scenario.question: Is the correlation between cost-per-unit and defects-per-unit a real operational signal, or something else?

decisions.prompt: Leadership wants you to validate the cost-cutting plan. How do you frame your investigation?

options.label: Validate the correlation with a regression
options.detail: Run a regression of defects-per-unit on cost-per-unit across plants to quantify the relationship.
options.consequence: The regression confirms a strong, statistically significant relationship — but you've fit a model to two ratios that share the same denominator. The math looks solid; the premise is not.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the team's hypothesis and laundered a spurious correlation through a more sophisticated method.

options.label: Diagnostic decomposition by plant volume
options.detail: Before trusting the ratio correlation, decompose each metric into its raw numerators and check whether plant volume explains the pattern.
options.consequence: You immediately see that the plants with the highest ratios are the lowest-volume plants — the shared denominator is inflating both metrics together. The correlation is an artifact, not a signal.

options.label: Interview plant managers about cost-cutting and quality trade-offs
options.detail: Gather qualitative evidence from managers about whether their cost-reduction efforts affected defect rates.
options.consequence: Managers give plausible stories in both directions. Qualitative evidence is useful color, but it can't resolve whether the correlation is real or a mathematical artifact.
options.divergenceCost: Sought qualitative validation for a correlation whose validity hadn't been tested quantitatively.

options.label: Benchmark the highest-cost, highest-defect plants for a fix
options.detail: Identify the worst-performing plants on both ratios and treat them as the intervention targets.
options.consequence: You've targeted the lowest-volume plants for intervention. But their ratios are high because they produce few units, not because they are operationally broken — the fix would address the wrong problem.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to intervention before checking whether the metric identified the right plants.

decisions.prompt: You've decided to look at volume. Which metric do you use to assess whether the correlation is real?

artifact.title: Cost-per-unit vs. Defects-per-unit correlation — plant-level ratios
artifact.caption: Both ratios are high for low-volume plants and low for high-volume plants. But is this cost driving defects, or a shared denominator at work?

options.label: The ratio correlation itself (cost-per-unit vs. defects-per-unit)
options.detail: Continue using the per-unit ratios as the evidence base, since they normalize for scale.
options.consequence: The correlation holds — because both ratios still share units-produced in the denominator. Normalizing for scale is exactly what created the artifact; using the ratios as evidence doesn't resolve the question.
options.divergenceCost: Used the artifact-generating metrics as evidence of their own validity.

options.label: Raw total costs and raw total defects, plotted against plant volume
options.detail: Strip the denominator out and look at absolute costs, absolute defects, and units produced separately across plants.
options.consequence: Plotted against volume, raw costs and raw defects do NOT move together — high-volume plants have high absolute costs but low absolute defects. The per-unit correlation vanishes when the shared denominator is removed.

artifact.title: Raw defect counts by plant volume tier (denominator removed)
artifact.caption: Raw defect counts are nearly flat across volume tiers. Low-volume plants look worse only because their unit count shrinks the denominator — not because they produce more defects.

decisions.prompt: The raw numerators don't co-move. The ratio correlation is likely a shared-denominator artifact. What do you tell leadership?

options.label: "The correlation is spurious — cost-cutting will not reduce defects. Cancel the initiative."
options.detail: Make the definitive call and advise against the plan.
options.consequence: You've correctly identified a likely artifact but overreached. It's possible some real cost-quality link exists within volume tiers that this analysis didn't fully rule out — and recommending cancellation without a confirmatory step leaves leadership with nowhere to go.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed a definitive causal conclusion from a single decomposition and offered no confirmatory path.

options.label: "The correlation appears to be a shared-denominator artifact, not a real cost-quality link — we should verify by analyzing plants within similar volume tiers before acting on it."
options.detail: Present the finding, name the mechanism, and recommend a confirmatory within-tier analysis before committing to the initiative.
options.consequence: You've reframed the team's assumption with a concrete mechanism, shown the evidence cleanly, and prescribed a next step that can confirm or refute the finding. Leadership gets a finding AND a decision-ready path forward.

insight: The strong correlation between cost-per-unit and defects-per-unit was entirely explained by plant volume: low-volume plants inflate both ratios simultaneously because the shared denominator (units produced) is small. When raw numerators were examined, the relationship disappeared. The lesson is that ratios sharing a denominator will tend to correlate even when their numerators are unrelated — always strip the denominator out and check volumes before treating a ratio correlation as a real signal.
